About

# Philosophy quotations, traced to where they were written

Philosophy Defined records where a quotation comes from — the work, the passage, the original language — and says plainly how much of that has been checked.

696 passages from 146 thinkers and texts, across Greco-Roman, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, Jewish, Japanese, and Africana traditions.

## What the archive is for

Philosophy quotations circulate detached from their sources, and many of the most shared ones were never written by the person they are credited to. This archive exists to answer the question a careful reader asks next: where exactly does this come from, and does the English say what the original says?

## How much has been checked

Every quotation page states which of the four levels below it has reached. The levels are one vocabulary used across the whole archive — the homepage, the editorial policy, and each passage's own status line all read them from the same register — so a page never claims a check it has not performed.

-   **Original text checked — 57 passages.** Checked against the cited edition, and the wording in the author's own language recorded beside the English.
-   **Edition checked — 1 passage.** Checked against the cited edition, with the circulating variants and the attribution note; no original-language text is recorded in the register yet.
-   **Annotated — 152 passages.** A source locator plus commentary written for the passage; the wording has not yet been collated against an edition.
-   **Recorded — 486 passages.** The English wording and the source as the corpus records them; not yet collated, and kept out of search results until the page carries writing of its own.

## How a record is built

Each passage is filed with its thinker, work, locator, school, and themes. Locators use the reference system scholars use for that author — Stephanus numbers for Plato, Bekker numbers for Aristotle, book and passage for the Analects, section numbers for Nietzsche — so a reader can find the passage in any edition. The details are in the [sourcing method](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method); selection and correction rules are in the [editorial policy](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy).

## Where to start

If you are holding a quotation and want to know who said it, use [the quote source finder](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source). To read by person, begin with [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) or [Nietzsche](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/friedrich-nietzsche); by subject, with [the self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) or [love](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/about/love); by work, with [the Meditations](https://www.philosophydef.com/works/meditations) or the [index of works](https://www.philosophydef.com/works). For background, the [guides](https://www.philosophydef.com/what-is-philosophy) and the [glossary of terms](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) explain the vocabulary.

## Editor

**kyree**. Maintains Philosophy Defined and the source records in this archive.

## Corrections

Attributions and locators are corrected when they are found to be wrong, and each correction is listed with its date in the [corrections log](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy#corrections-log). To report an error, write to [kyreemeng@gmail.com](mailto:kyreemeng@gmail.com) with the page address and the edition you are checking against.

## Why “Philosophy Defined”?

The name says what the archive is for. A quotation is only worth reading once you know where it comes from: which book, which passage, which translation, and whether the person credited with it actually said it. So each record here is traced to its source, and the common misattributions are registered rather than repeated. The [source lookup](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) and the [random generator](https://www.philosophydef.com/random-philosophy-generator) are both still here; the generator is simply the front door to the same archive.
